title: Security and Fire Alarm Systems Installers

bls.growth: O*NET summary page shows projected growth of about 7% or more through 2035; BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook has no profile page for this occupation (the OOH electrical installers page does not cover it)
bls.medianPay: $56,430 per year, $27.13 per hour (May 2023 OEWS); O*NET page shows a newer median of about $60,070 per year

summary: These workers install, program, maintain and repair wiring and equipment for burglar, access-control, video and fire alarm systems. They run low-voltage cable, mount panels, detectors and sirens, connect them, set them up, test them and show customers how they work. Most are employed by security-service firms and building-equipment contractors, and fire alarm work is tied to separate fire-protection standards.
typicalPath: O*NET Job Zone 3: about 49% hold a post-secondary certificate and 41% a high school diploma (onetonline.org summary page). Training is mostly on the job or through a contractor, plus manufacturer courses. About 38 states license fire alarm technicians, and roughly 29 require or accept NICET fire alarm certification (four levels, from about 6 months to 10 years of experience); where a state has no program, NFPA 72 still points to third-party certification such as NICET (securityinfowatch.com article via search results, not opened in full). Requirements vary by state and by security versus fire work.

tasks.task: Install, maintain and repair security systems, alarm devices and related equipment following electrical drawings and building plans.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Reading device layouts; basic circuit knowledge; NEC Articles 725, 760, 800 for the wiring.

tasks.task: Mount control panels, sensors and cameras and connect the wiring between system parts.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Equipment mounting, enclosure and termination practice; working space and access around panels.

tasks.task: Demonstrate system operation to customers and explain causes of false alarms.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Understanding of how detectors and keypads behave; communication skills rather than code.

tasks.task: Test circuits and detection devices and correct faults against the specifications.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Meter use, continuity, voltage and resistance checks, supervision of circuits.

tasks.task: Pull cable through walls, attics and cavities to outlet points, then position and terminate it.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Cable routing and support, separation from power wiring, fire-stopping penetrations (NEC 760, 725, 800, 300.21).

tasks.task: Diagnose systems to find problems such as disconnected components or damaged shielding.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Troubleshooting open, short and ground faults on signaling circuits.

tasks.task: Check backup power, keypads, alarms and other features for correct operation or faults.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Standby battery capacity checks, trouble signals, loop supervision (NFPA 72 for fire).

tasks.task: Drill holes in walls, floors and framing so wiring can pass through.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Protecting cables near framing, firestopping and not drilling into live wiring (NEC 300.4, 300.21 apply where referenced).

tasks.task: Review work orders and blueprints to decide materials and installation methods.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Plan and device-layout reading; identifying circuit classes before routing.

tasks.task: Discuss security concerns with customers and set system requirements.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Matching devices to risk; little direct code content.

tasks.task: Install conduit and raceway and secure cables with fastening tools.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Raceway selection, fill and support; fire alarm cable fastening intervals (NEC 760, Chapter 3 where referenced).

tasks.task: Adjust device sensitivity to room conditions using programming controls.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Panel programming, device addressing, sensitivity settings; NFPA 72 sets limits for fire detectors.

tasks.task: Keep up with new products and technology, order parts, prepare warranty paperwork and cost estimates.
tasks.electricalKnowledge: Product listing awareness (UL 864 and 681 listed equipment); estimating.

procedures.name: Electrically safe work for line-voltage connections
procedures.purpose: Make the supply to a panel, power supply or transformer dead and prove it before touching it.
procedures.whenUsed: Whenever a fire or security panel, power supply or other equipment is wired to or served from a line-voltage circuit.
procedures.role: Installer (qualified person) with the facility electrician or owner's authorized employee.
steps: Find the circuit that feeds the equipment and tell affected people the work is planned.
Switch off the circuit and open the disconnecting means; for fire alarm panels note that this removes protection, so arrange impairment steps first.
Apply a lock and tag to the disconnect, or use the equivalent measure if a lock cannot be fitted.
Release or restrain any stored energy, including backup batteries on the panel.
Test with a meter that works, check the circuit at the work point, then recheck the meter.
Do the work, keeping to required approach distances and using insulated tools.
Before restoring power, remove tools, check people are clear, remove locks and tags, then re-energize and confirm normal status.
hazards: Loss of fire protection while the panel is off
controls: Insulated tools and PPE chosen by hazard assessment
Impairment notification when a fire system is off

standards.name: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.333
standards.what: Deenergize live parts where possible, lock and tag the disconnect, verify dead with tests, check before re-energizing.

standards.name: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147
standards.what: General lockout/tagout program for servicing machinery: written procedures, training, annual inspection.

standards.name: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.132
standards.what: Employer must assess hazards and supply and train workers on fitting PPE.

standards.name: NFPA 70E (copyrighted)
standards.what: Electrical safe work condition and arc-flash practices; applicability to low-voltage alarm panels is limited but the supply side counts.

evidence.says: Lock and tag disconnects, verify de-energized state including backfeed, and inspect before re-energizing.
Isolate, lock or tag, release stored energy and verify before servicing; annual procedure inspection.
Hazard assessment and PPE training are employer duties.

procedures.appCoverage: partial: the app teaches why disconnects and shock protection matter and where the means must be, but not the lockout, testing-before-touching or re-energizing steps.

procedures.name: Plan reading and device layout check
procedures.purpose: Work out where devices, panels and cable runs go and which circuits they use before pulling cable.
procedures.whenUsed: At job start, from the work order, drawings and building plans.
procedures.role: Installer or lead installer, with the designer or project manager.
steps: Read the work order and scope, and confirm the system type (fire, intrusion, access control, video).
Check the approved shop drawings and device layout against the building plans.
Mark panel, power supply, device and annunciator locations, checking mounting and access space.
Plan cable routes, noting fire-rated walls, ceilings and spaces where firestopping or plenum cable is needed.
Identify each circuit's class (power-limited fire alarm, Class 2/3, non-power-limited, communications) and plan separation from power wiring.
List materials and quantities, and raise conflicts with the designer before drilling.
hazards: Drilling into live wiring or structure
Wrong cable type in a plenum or fire-rated assembly
controls: Layout reviewed with designer or inspector

standards.name: NFPA 72 (copyrighted)
standards.what: Sets device placement and spacing for fire alarm design; drawings are the basis for acceptance.

standards.name: NEC Article 760 / 725 / 800
standards.what: Circuit class and cable type determine the wiring method and separation.

evidence.says: Installers review work orders and blueprints to decide materials and installation methods.
Acceptance testing expects approved shop drawings and a device layout to be on hand.

procedures.appCoverage: none: the app has no plan-reading or layout tasks; wiring-methods covers only the wiring rules.

procedures.name: Running low-voltage and fire alarm cable and raceway
procedures.purpose: Route, support, separate and identify signaling cable so it stays safe and trouble-free.
procedures.whenUsed: During rough-in, for new work and additions.
procedures.role: Systems installer or technician, working to the plans and the employer's written procedure.
steps: Choose cable of the right listed type for the circuit and the space (riser, plenum, general).
Keep fire alarm and Class 2/3 conductors out of enclosures and raceways with power or Class 1 conductors unless separated by a barrier or the approved exception applies.
Route through or along framing with the specified clearance or a protective plate.
Support cable with secure fastening at the required intervals and keep the work neat.
Firestop penetrations through fire-rated assemblies.
Label circuits at junction points so other work does not trigger signals, and remove abandoned cable.
Check the run for damage before termination.
hazards: Cable damage or short against power conductors
Shock hazard if a fault crosses to line voltage

standards.name: NEC Article 760
standards.what: Fire alarm circuits: power-limited and non-power-limited rules, separation, support and identification.

standards.name: NEC Articles 725 and 800
standards.what: Class 2/3 and communications circuits: cable types and separation from power wiring.

standards.name: NEC 300.21 and 300.22
standards.what: Fire-rated openings and ducts or plenum spaces where Article 760 refers to them.

standards.name: NFPA 72 (copyrighted)
standards.what: Circuit survivability and pathway class (supervision, survivability) for fire alarm wiring.

evidence.says: PLFA cable cannot share enclosures with power conductors without barrier; support, framing protection and circuit identification rules.
Installers thread cable through walls, attics and cavities and install conduit.

procedures.appCoverage: partial: wiring-methods trains routing and support in power wiring, but not signaling circuit classes, listed cable types or low-voltage separation.

procedures.name: Installing panels, devices and power supply connections
procedures.purpose: Mount and connect panels, detectors, notification devices and security devices, and supply the panel correctly.
procedures.role: Installer; a licensed electrician may do the line-voltage feed depending on the state.
steps: Mount the panel and power supply at the planned location with working space and access.
Confirm the feed comes from a dedicated branch circuit with a marked disconnect and no GFCI or AFCI protection where the NEC forbids it.
Connect devices and terminate conductors, keeping circuit polarity and supervision correct.
Ground metal enclosures and connect equipment grounding conductors.
Install batteries last, only when ready to test.
Mount detectors, horns, strobes, pull stations and sensors at the layout locations.
Label the panel, circuits and the feed disconnect.
controls: Procedure 1 before work on the feed
Dedicated, marked fire alarm branch circuit

standards.name: NEC Article 760
standards.what: Fire alarm branch circuit: dedicated, red-marked disconnect, restricted access, no GFCI or AFCI.

standards.name: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.304
standards.what: Wiring design: disconnecting means, grounding and identification of conductors.

standards.name: UL 864 and UL 681 (copyrighted)
standards.what: Product and installation listings for fire alarm control units and burglar alarm systems.

standards.name: NFPA 70 Article 110
standards.what: Working space and workmanship rules where they apply to panels and enclosures.

evidence.says: PLFA supply: dedicated circuit, red disconnect marked FIRE ALARM CIRCUIT, restricted access, no GFCI or AFCI.
Disconnecting means, grounding and conductor identification apply to wiring design.
Installers mount control panels, sensors and cameras and connect their wiring.

procedures.appCoverage: partial: the app trains panel installation, working space, grounding and marking for power panels but not alarm panels, supervised circuits or battery handling.

procedures.name: Programming, addressing and sensitivity adjustment
procedures.purpose: Make devices known to the panel and set them so they report correctly without false alarms.
procedures.whenUsed: After device installation and before testing, and after changes.
steps: Assign addresses or zones to each device per the point list and drawings.
Enter device types, labels and zone text in the panel from the approved sequence of operations.
Set outputs, notification and monitoring communication settings.
Adjust detector sensitivity to the room within the allowed range.
Back up the programming and record the version.
Check that each point shows the correct label before functional testing.
hazards: Wrong zone leading to wrong location reported

standards.name: NFPA 72 (copyrighted)
standards.what: Reacceptance testing is needed after software changes and when devices are added or deleted.

standards.name: UL 864 (copyrighted)
standards.what: Listing covers control unit behavior and settings of listed panels.

evidence.says: Installers adjust device sensitivity to room conditions using programming controls.
Remote annunciators must show the correct point and condition matching approved plans.

procedures.appCoverage: none: the app has no panel or device programming content.

procedures.name: Functional and acceptance testing with documentation
procedures.purpose: Show every device and the standby power work, and record the result for the authority having jurisdiction and owner.
procedures.whenUsed: After installation and programming, and again after any added, deleted or modified components.
procedures.role: Installer or certified technician, with the owner and the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) or inspector.
steps: Confirm approved drawings, sequence of operations and the battery calculation are on hand.
Check wiring and insulation for faults and verify circuit supervision by creating open and ground conditions.
Test pull stations, smoke and heat detectors by approved methods, and supervisory inputs such as waterflow and tamper.
Verify audible and visible notification appliances operate across the coverage area.
Test standby battery condition and capacity and check the system survives the required standby period.
Confirm alarm, supervisory and trouble signals reach the panel, annunciators and monitoring service.
Record deficiencies and correct them, reset to normal, and obtain the inspector's sign-off.
Deliver records and train the owner.
hazards: False dispatch to the fire department
Shock from live equipment during testing
controls: Notify monitoring company and building occupants before testing

standards.name: NFPA 72 Chapter 14 (copyrighted)
standards.what: Acceptance, reacceptance and periodic inspection, testing and maintenance requirements, including tables of methods and intervals.

standards.name: Fire code (IFC or NFPA 1) and AHJ rules
standards.what: Requires the system to be tested and maintained and sets who must witness or receive records.

evidence.says: Acceptance covers device tests, notification, battery and standby duration, signals, deficiency list and inspector sign-off.
NFPA 72 Chapter 14 covers testing and maintenance, with owners responsible for upkeep after acceptance.

procedures.appCoverage: none: the app has no testing, meter or acceptance-inspection tasks.

procedures.name: Impairment handling and restoration
procedures.purpose: Control the risk and tell the right people when a fire alarm system or part is out of service.
procedures.whenUsed: When a system is turned off for service, a fault takes devices out, or work lasts beyond a short period.
procedures.role: Impairment coordinator (owner or designated person) with the service technician.
steps: Notify the coordinator before the system is taken out of service and agree scope and duration.
Inform the fire department, owner, insurer and monitoring company as the plan requires.
Use a fire watch or other interim measures for longer outages.
Tag the affected equipment as out of service.
Complete the repair and run the tests needed to prove the affected parts work.
Notify all parties that protection is restored and remove the tag.
controls: Notification to the fire department and others

standards.name: NFPA 72 Chapter 14 / NFPA 25 (copyrighted)
standards.what: Impairment coordinator duties, notification and restoration steps (NFPA 25 for sprinklers, 72 for fire alarm).

standards.name: Local fire code and insurer requirements
standards.what: Set when the fire department must be told and when a fire watch is required.

evidence.says: Coordinator verifies scope, notifies fire department and insurer, uses fire watch, tags equipment and confirms restoration.
Fire codes place the maintenance obligation on owners, supported by an approved testing program.

procedures.appCoverage: none: nothing in the app covers fire protection system outages or reporting.

standardsAndCodes.name: NFPA 70 (NEC) Article 760
standardsAndCodes.role: Wiring rules for fire alarm circuits, including power-limited and non-power-limited circuits, supply, separation and identification.

standardsAndCodes.name: NFPA 70 (NEC) Article 725
standardsAndCodes.role: Class 1, 2 and 3 remote-control and signaling circuits, used for many security and access-control circuits.

standardsAndCodes.name: NFPA 70 (NEC) Article 800
standardsAndCodes.role: Communications and network wiring used by monitoring and video systems.

standardsAndCodes.name: NFPA 72 National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code
standardsAndCodes.role: Design, installation performance, acceptance testing, inspection, testing and maintenance, and impairments for fire alarm systems.
standardsAndCodes.nec: Cross-referenced to Article 760 but not part of the NEC

standardsAndCodes.name: UL 864
standardsAndCodes.role: Product listing for fire alarm control units and accessories.

standardsAndCodes.name: UL 681
standardsAndCodes.role: Installation and classification of burglar and holdup alarm systems.

standardsAndCodes.name: NFPA 1 / IFC fire code, NFPA 101
standardsAndCodes.role: Require fire alarm systems to be installed, tested and maintained and reference NFPA 70 and 72.

standardsAndCodes.name: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147, 1910.333, 1910.132, 1910.304
standardsAndCodes.role: Lockout, electrical safe work practices, PPE and wiring design for the line-voltage side.

standardsAndCodes.name: NICET fire alarm certification and state licensing
standardsAndCodes.role: Qualification route for fire alarm technicians in many states.

outsideNec: Fire alarm design, device spacing, notification performance and acceptance, inspection and maintenance: NFPA 72, not the NEC.
Product listing of panels and devices: UL 864 (fire) and UL 681 (burglar), plus central-station and monitoring standards such as UL 827.
Fire code duties for owners, impairments, fire watch and AHJ witnessing: NFPA 1, International Fire Code, local amendments.
Licensing, certification and permits: state and local rules, NICET.
Programming, addressing and manufacturer instructions: vendor documentation.
Security-specific work (cameras, access control, network setup) follows manufacturer instructions and often IT standards, with only the wiring under the NEC.
gapsForTheApp: Low-voltage and fire alarm circuits: classes (Class 2/3, power-limited and non-power-limited fire alarm, communications), cable types and separation are not taught; a Chapter 7 and 8 skill is needed.
Fire alarm systems: panel, initiating and notification devices, supervision, battery and standby power are not in the app.
Testing with a meter and functional testing: no continuity, voltage or loop-check tasks.
Acceptance testing and documentation: no scenario type for walking a system through a witnessed test and filling the record.
Impairment procedures and AHJ notification: no content.
Lockout/tagout and testing before touching: absent, although the occupation connects panels to line voltage.
Plan and device-layout reading: no drawing-based tasks.
Programming and addressing: no panel interface simulation.
Firestopping and cable routing through fire-rated assemblies: not taught.
Cross-code content: the NEC content policy needs a way to link NFPA 72 and UL topics as outside-code items.
doubts: No BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook page exists for this occupation; the OOH page was not available (HTTP 403 for the guessed URL, and the electrical installers page does not cover it), so growth and openings come from O*NET text and are not confirmed. Pay and employment use the OEWS May 2023 page.
O*NET summary page shows a median of $60,070 and 86,300 employees, which differs from OEWS May 2023; the year of the O*NET figures was not shown.
The O*NET task list was retrieved through a summarizing fetch; importance scores should be rechecked on the page before quoting them.

NFPA 72, NFPA 70E, UL 864 and UL 681 are paywalled; descriptions come from secondary pages and search snippets, not the standards. The UL pages (globalspec, ANSI) appeared in search results but were not opened.

NEC Article 725 and 800 separation rules come from a search summary (ecmweb, industrialmonitordirect, Mike Holt); only the ecmweb Article 760 page was opened. The Mike Holt PDF and the Minnesota health department PDF could not be read.
The licensing and NICET numbers come from a search summary of securityinfowatch.com and getlicensemap, not opened pages.

Procedures with only one fully relevant opened source beyond O*NET: programming and addressing (O*NET plus the acceptance checklist, which only touches annunciator points) and plan reading (O*NET plus the acceptance checklist). Impairment steps come from a college page and a trade article, not NFPA 72 itself.
The Bates page is a campus procedure that is mostly about sprinkler impairments (NFPA 25); applicability to alarm-only impairments follows NFPA 72 Chapter 14 per search results.
Which tasks require a licensed electrician versus an alarm installer for the line-voltage feed varies by state and was not confirmed.
